questions.question: What is the practical meaning of calling a vector space finite-dimensional?
options: It can be generated by finitely many vectors.
It contains only finitely many distinct vectors.
Each vector is a finite combination of some vectors.
Its vectors are lists with finitely many entries.

questions.question: Why is $\mathbb{R}^2$ finite-dimensional?
options: Every vector in it has length $2$.
It has no scalar multiplication.
It contains only two vectors.

questions.question: Does finite-dimensional mean that the vector space has finitely many vectors?
options: Yes; finitely many spanning vectors give finitely many sums.
No; $\mathbb{R}^2$ has infinitely many vectors but dimension $2$.
Yes; dimension $n$ means the space holds exactly $n$ vectors.
No; it means each vector has finitely many nonzero entries.

questions.question: What role do bases and spanning lists play in a finite-dimensional vector space?
options: They make every vector equal to zero.
They control how vectors are represented.
They remove vector addition from the space.
They replace scalars by matrices.

questions.question: Which kind of list is enough to show that a vector space is finite-dimensional?
options: An infinite list of unrelated scalars.
A list of every vector in the space.
A finite spanning list.
A list containing only the zero vector, regardless of the space.

questions.question: Why does $((1,0),(0,1))$ show that $\mathbb{R}^2$ is finite-dimensional?
options: It shows that $\mathbb{R}^2$ has only two elements.
It lists every vector in $\mathbb{R}^2$.
It is a finite list that spans $\mathbb{R}^2$.
It contains no scalar coefficients.

questions.question: The space of polynomials of degree at most $2$ has basis $(1,x,x^2)$. What does this show?
options: It is finite-dimensional.
It has no spanning list.
It contains only three polynomials.
It is not a vector space.

questions.question: If $V=\operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2)$, what can be concluded about $V$?
options: $V$ is finite-dimensional.
$V$ cannot contain the zero vector.
$V$ contains exactly two vectors.
$V$ has no basis.

questions.question: A line through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is spanned by one nonzero vector. What does this imply?
options: The line cannot be a vector space.
The line is not closed under scalar multiplication.
The line is finite-dimensional.
The line contains only one vector.

questions.question: If a vector space has a finite spanning list of $4$ vectors, what is safe to conclude?
options: It contains exactly $4$ vectors.
It is finite-dimensional.
Its dimension must be exactly $4$.
Every spanning list has length $4$.

questions.question: Why can a spanning list be longer than the dimension of the space?
options: Because dimension is the length of the longest spanning list.
Because a basis only has to span, not be independent.
Because a spanning list may contain redundant vectors.
Because the dimension changes with the spanning list chosen.

questions.question: What does finite-dimensionality allow us to do with vector-representation problems?
options: Reduce to finitely many basis coefficients.
Write each vector as a multiple of one basis vector.
Use coefficients that do not depend on the basis.
Check only finitely many vectors in the space.

questions.question: Does a finite-dimensional vector space have to come from geometry such as $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: Yes; spaces of polynomials are always infinite-dimensional.
No; polynomials of degree at most $2$ also form an example.
Yes; only Euclidean spaces $\mathbb{R}^n$ can be finite-dimensional.
No, but other examples must contain finitely many vectors.

questions.question: If $V=\operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, which conclusion is justified?
options: $V$ has dimension exactly $3$.
$V$ contains exactly $3$ vectors.
$V$ has no basis because the list might be redundant.
$V$ is finite-dimensional, with dimension at most $3$.

questions.question: If a vector space has a basis of length $5$, what follows?
options: Every spanning list of it has exactly five vectors.
It contains exactly five vectors, the basis ones.
It must be $\mathbb{R}^5$ with the standard basis.
It is finite-dimensional of dimension $5$.

questions.question: Why is $\mathbb{R}^n$ finite-dimensional?
options: Each of its vectors has finitely many nonzero entries.
Every vector in it is a multiple of one fixed vector.
It contains just $n$ vectors, namely the standard ones.
Spanned by the $n$ standard coordinate vectors.

questions.question: Can a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ contain infinitely many vectors?
options: Only when its dimension is at least $2$, never for lines.
No; finite-dimensional means finitely many vectors.
Yes; it means finitely many directions, not elements.
Yes, but only when the scalars are complex numbers.

questions.question: Why does a finite spanning list not necessarily give the dimension immediately?
options: The vector space might not contain zero.
The list may contain redundant vectors.
The list cannot contain scalar multiples.
The list must be infinite first.

questions.question: If $W=\operatorname{span}(w_1,w_2,w_3)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^4$, what dimension bound is guaranteed?
options: $\dim(W)\le 3$
$\dim(W)=3$ always
$\dim(W)=0$ always

questions.question: The polynomial space with basis $(1,x,x^2)$ is used. Which polynomial is outside the space of degree at most $2$?
